Legally striking 
CRU anticipated that in Q4 2009 there was going to be turmoil regarding negotiations of collective labour 
agreements at several major copper mine operations.  A few weeks ago, the attention was focused on the 
start-up of negotiations at BHP Billiton’s Spence mine as it was expected to set a precedent for further 
bargaining at major operations including Escondida (BHP Billiton, Rio Tinto, JECO and IFC) and 
Chuquicamata (Codelco).  These two are of especial interest as the negotiations will overlap with the 
forthcoming presidential elections.  Early proposals from the managers of BHP Billiton and Codelco, 
however, and an uneasy environment at Spence have shaken up the market, whilst these actions have 
been raising supply-side concerns in the copper market. Likewise, the copper price reached the highest 
level in 13 months, and this encourages the claims of the mine workers. 
In this report, we aim to go briefly through the main issues of the Chilean recent collective labour 
agreements, their respective negotiations and the legal timeline of the negotiations process. Our main 
findings are: 
 The early offer accepted by the unionised workers at Escondida (operated by BHP Billiton) set a 
precedent as it has been the most generous deal for a collective labour agreement ever seen in Chile.  
 Copper mines in Chile that have pending negotiations for collective labour agreements account for 
20% of the Chilean copper mine production.  
 The Chilean labour legislation sets a legal framework for unionised workers to negotiate their 
collective labour agreements.  The legislation is not exclusive to the mining industry. In the second 
section of the report we describe, in a simplified version, the timeline of the negotiations for a 
collective labour agreement in Chile. The overall process – from the start of the official negotiations 
to the end of a likely longest strike period – can take as long as 85 days.

Family (and neighbours) ties 
In Q3 2006, unionised workers at Escondida held a 25-day strike before agreeing a collective labour 
contract with the company.  This strike was the longest and most harmful – in terms of production losses 
– for the industry in the recent Chilean history.  In 2009, a similar scenario was expected as negotiations 
were due to start in early December, just a week before the presidential elections in Chile. However, an 
early offer to renew the collective labour agreement made by the managers was approved by 72% of the 
unionised workers.  The offer at Escondida is the most generous ever seen in Chile: end-of-conflict bonus 
of around US$25,500 
per worker (the 
highest of the recent 
history, see table), a 
one time 5% increase 
of wages, 44-month 
duration, social 
benefits for their 
families and access to 
a US$6,300 loan with 
highly favourable 
terms. As a reference, 
the US$25,500 bonus 
is roughly between 
two and three times 
Chile’s GDP per capita, and would be considerably higher than an annual wage of an average worker in 
any other industry in Chile. 
In October 2009, aggressive negotiations reached a staltement at BHP Billiton’s Spence mine.  The mine 
started-up in 2006 and the first collective labour agreement expired in September 2009.  Unionised 
workers at Spence rejected offers made by the company’s management and have been on strike since 
October 13th, although there was an attempt to resume negotiations.  The workers demands, according to 
press reports, consist of: 5.5% increase in wages, 24-month duration and US$27,250 bonuses 
(~US$13,750 per year). This is more ambitious than the deal recently reached at Escondida, and higher 
than the latest agreements of other copper mines in Chile (see table).  
CRU considers that BHP Billiton will be able to withstand the strike at Spence for a considerable period.  
The 25-day strike at Escondida set a benchmark, although it is not fully owned by BHP Billiton.  
Escondida produces six times more copper than Spence. The copper cash price in August 2006 
(US$7,696/t) was 24% higher than the one in October 2009 (US$6,267/t as of 28th October).  The market 
value of the production that was lost in 2006 was broadly US$317M (US$182M attributable to BHP 
Billiton), and 16-day strike at Spence can be around US$48M (as of 29th October). 
Codelco Norte and Andina (two of the five mine operations of Codelco) will negotiate the renewal of 
their collective labour agreements in December 2009.  For many people, the Escondida agreement sets a

However, Codelco is a state-owned company, has a lower productivity and higher costs. Therefore, in this 
case, the presidential elections are more relevant than for other mines.  
The mines that are due to negotiate collective labour agreements in the next few months are expected to 
produce, altogether, 20% of the Chilean or 6% of the world’s copper mine production in 2009.  A list of 
2009 negotiations at South American mines is available in the June 2009 edition of the CRU Copper 
South America Monthly. 
Timeline for the negotiations  
 In Chile, the collective labour agreements are ruled by the labour, not the mining, authorities.  Therefore, 
the same legal framework applies across every industry.  However, it has the greatest impact at copper 
mines, as workers 
are aware that 
mining companies 
are earning higher 
profits at the current 
copper price. The 
negotiation process 
can take as long as 
85 days (including a 
strike) and during 
this time is unlikely 
that employees 
would work at their

productivity (see 
table). Collective 
labour agreements 
have to last between 2 and 4 years.  It can be understood that companies will aim to agree for longer 
periods, in order to delay the negotiation process. 
Copper production 
 In Chile, copper production increased 8% y-o-y in August according to Cochilco.  This is the first 
increase after thirteen consecutive months of declines. Codelco produced 22,400t more because of 
Gaby reaching full production and increases in all divisions except Andina. Escondida increased its 
production to 100,000t (12,200t more than August 2008) due to the restart of its SAG mill at Laguna 
Seca concentrator. In addition, Spence and Collahuasi showed over 5,000t increases respect to August 
2008. Meanwhile, Candelaria decreased its production in 9,300t. 
In September, according to the National Statistics Institute, copper production in Chile was 464,555t 
(8.5% y-o-y).   
 In Peru, copper production decreased in September in 2% y-o-y.  Antamina’s production declined by 
14% (4,300t) to 26,600t; which was offset by y-o-y increases in production at Cerro Corona (2,500t 
more than in September 2008 as it reaches full capacity), Toquepala (2,600t) and Cerro Verde 
(3,600t).  All other mines showed minor variations.
